about: The words of the chain cnut_1016 (Data/encounters/chain_cnut_1016_793.json; Design/content/chains/cnut_1016.md): Cnut's peace from the tribute of 1018 to the king's death in 1035, and his letter of 1027 on the tolls taken from merchants and pilgrims. Every title, intention, line and label key of the thirteen cards, an outcome for every option (out_<option>, with _success and _failure where there is a chance), the news the chain spreads, and an art.<card id> line for every card. No words are quoted from any translation: the Chronicle and the king's letter are given in our own rendering. A draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The weighing

The tribute is being gathered over all England, and the town's share is weighed out on a bench by the water. The reeve's man goes from door to door and from keel to keel. The fleet lies in the river and waits.
Seventy-two thousand pounds from the whole land, and ten thousand five hundred more from this town alone. We held the wall against him all one summer. This is what holding it costs.
Seventy-two thousand pounds from the whole land, and Lunden pays its own on top. Our share is on that bench. It is short, as you can see by my face.
You are a stranger and owe nothing. I only say that the men who pay now will be the men this town knows afterwards.
They told us Michaelmas. Then Martinmas. A man can drink a town dry while he waits to be paid for not burning it.
When it is weighed we go home, all but forty ships. I have a farm in Jutland I have not seen in five winters. I hope my wife has.
Lay down sixty pennies toward the town's share
Sell drink and cloth to the men who are waiting for their pay
Say you are a stranger here, and watch the weighing
The reeve's man cuts a notch for you among the townsmen, and asks how your name is said so that he can say it to the reeve. Sixty pennies go into the scale. They do not move it much.
The shipmen buy on trust against their pay, and the first of them puts thirty pennies in your hand to show the trust is good. Ale and wine will be dear here until the fleet has sailed.

You watch a kingdom being weighed in a fish scale. The man at the beam, to pass the time, asks you a riddle about a thing that was earth once and hid in the earth, and that earth can now be bought with.

A waterside in grey autumn light: a bench with a great balance and sacks of pennies, a reeve's man with a tally stick, townspeople in a line; behind them longships moored in rows across the river, their crews sitting idle on the rowing benches.
Irons for Denmark

The fleet has gone home and forty ships lie below the bridge. A moneyer of the town stands on the hythe with a locked chest and a boy. The king wants English pennies struck among the Danes, and the irons to strike them are in the chest.
Leofstan, moneyer. I am to go to Ripa in Jutland and strike the king's pennies there. The king's ships are all somewhere else. Are you bound east?
You are the stranger who paid toward the town's share. The reeve said to ask you first. He does not say that often.
You sold ale to the fleet in the year of the weighing. Then you know Danes, which is more than I do.
Two irons and a hammer. A man found with these and no leave loses his hand, so I would be glad if nobody dropped the chest in the river.
One king from this bridge to the Sound. A man can sail it now with a full hold and an empty sword-hand. Three winters ago I would have taken that chest from him.
Carry him and his chest to Ripa for forty pennies
Carry him for nothing but his good word at the king's mint
You are not bound for Jutland: ask what the king wants with English irons
He counts out forty pennies of his own striking and looks at each one as it goes. The boy sits on the chest the whole way and will not get off it to sleep.
He says a moneyer's word is the only thing he makes that nobody can clip. The boy sits on the chest the whole way and will not get off it to sleep.
The Danes have silver by the sackful and weigh it out in bits, he says. The king wants them to count it instead, with his face on every piece. A Dane takes him east on the next tide.

A timber hythe on the Thames on a bright morning: a neat man in a town cloak beside an iron-bound chest, a boy sitting on it; behind them the wooden bridge and a row of forty beached warships with their masts down.
One penny on both shores

At Ripa a hearth burns in a shed beside the bishop's church and a hammer rings on iron. The pennies come off the block with the king's head on one face and Ripa's name on the other. The same penny now buys ale on the Thames and on this river.
You see the chest came dry. Hold out your hand. That is the first one off the iron here; I kept it for the boat that brought me.
The shipman from the hythe. I came over with a Dane who sang the whole way. I have thought of your quiet boat more than once.
They still weigh them. I tell them the king has weighed them already. They nod, and then they weigh them.
Half of what the king takes in this town is the bishop's. The bishop says so. The king has not said otherwise, and we take that as a charter.
Bishop Odinkar was schooled over the sea and came home with a taste for Rhine wine at the altar and at table. Jutland grows neither. Six casks, and he pays as a bishop should.
Take the bishop's order: six casks of Rhine wine before next summer
Change your silver for the king's pennies at his table
Ask the moneyer what the Danes make of it
The clerk writes six casks on his tablet and the price beside it: half as much again as the market gives. The nearest vine is on the Rhine. He knows it, and so does the price.
Your mixed silver goes into the pot and the king's pennies come back by count. The toll man here takes them without reaching for his scales, and takes less while he is in a good temper about it.

They say a king's face is a strange thing to put on something a man must cut in half to buy a hen. Leofstan gives you a riddle about the thing they trust instead: twin sisters under one strict law, who favour no man and stand level only when both carry the same.

An open-fronted shed by a small timber church at Ribe, evening: the moneyer at a wooden block with hammer raised, a glowing hearth, a bishop's clerk with a wax tablet, and two Danes at the doorway weighing a new penny on folding scales.
As far as an axe is thrown

The king has given the haven at the Wantsum mouth and its tolls to Christ Church, on both shores. At high water a monk stands in a boat and a ship's boy throws a small axe at the land. Where it falls, the monks' right ends.
From a ship afloat at the top of the tide, as far inland as a small axe can be thrown. The king's own words. We did not ask for an axe; we would have said a bowshot.
It is all in the writing, with the king's cross and the queen's and the archbishop's. A toll without a writing is only a man with his hand out.
Before the monks I paid the king's reeve. Before him, his father. The hand changes. I have never yet seen it close.
They pick the boy with care. Last year's boy could have thrown it to Canterbury. This year's is the cellarer's nephew.
Pay the monks' toll and ask to see the writing
Ask to throw the axe yourself
Ask the ferryman what he paid before the monks came

He holds the leaf where you can see it and reads it out, a finger under each word. The names of the witnesses run longer than the gift. You pay the toll, and you know now what a toll looks like when it has a king behind it.

The axe turns over twice in the sun and stands in the turf a good three paces past the boy's mark. The monk moves his stake without a word against it, and is easy about your toll for the rest of the season.
The axe goes into the water a boat's length short of the shore. The ferryman says the monks should hire you every year. Your crew is still telling it at supper.
The same, he says, to the halfpenny. The king gave away the toll; he did not make it lighter. But the monks write down who has paid, and the reeve never did, so now a man pays only once.

High tide in a wide flat haven under a big sky at noon: a small boat with a monk standing in it and a boy caught in the act of throwing a hand axe toward a low green shore; a ferry and a moored trading ship behind, gulls overhead.
The third toll

On the toll bank below the wall of Cologne eleven people sit on their bundles: English and Danes bound for Rome, and two men of Lunden with cloth. The toll man has taken toll from all of them as merchants. It is the third time since the river mouth.
A pilgrim goes free. A pilgrim with four bolts of cloth is a merchant with a staff. I did not put the cloth on his back.
The cloth is to eat with. It is forty days to Rome from here, and nobody on this river feeds a Dane for his prayers.
A tenth at the count's water. Pennies for the showing at Tiel. A tenth again here. At this rate I shall come to the mountains owning my shoes.
At home we have one king from the Thames to the Sound and one toll at each end. Here every man with a rope across the river is a king.
Wine for a bishop in Jutland? Then you will pay the tenth on it, as bishops' wine has always paid here, and I will give you a tally to say so.
Pay the pilgrims' toll yourself: forty-five pennies
Speak for them: the cloth is their bread, not their trade
Say nothing: count what he takes and cut it on a stick

The toll man gives the cloth back and takes your pennies instead; it is all one to him. The old Dane, Toke, asks the name of your boat and says it over until he has it. You cut the count on a stick: three tolls, and what each took.

You ask the toll man whether he would sell his own dinner. He looks at the pilgrims' feet for a while, gives back the cloth and keeps the merchants' tenth. You cut the count on a stick: three tolls, and what each took.

The toll man hears you out and then charges you ten pennies for showing your own goods on his bank while you talked. The pilgrims go on a bolt lighter. You cut the count on a stick, your ten pennies with it.
You stand by the mooring post and cut notches: three tolls since the sea, and what each took from eleven people. Nobody asks what the stick is for. Shipmen are always cutting something.

A muddy river bank under a high Roman wall on a wet afternoon: pilgrims with staffs and scrips sitting on bundles of cloth, a toll man at a trestle with a balance and a rope strung to a post, river barges moored behind, a shipman in the foreground notching a stick.
The count's water

Since the count beat the emperor's army in the marsh at Flardinga, his men sit at the river mouth and take what they please from every keel bound for England. The merchants of Tiel have sent to the emperor twice. They are loading in one company, and there is room in it.
The emperor sent a duke and a bishop with an army. The marsh kept the army and the count kept the marsh. Now he has a toll and a victory, and we have a grievance.
We told the emperor plainly: if this stands, we cannot go to Britain and the Britons cannot come to us, and then your own tolls at Tiel are worth nothing. He understood the last part.
There are creeks behind the island a small keel can take on the night flood. I say can. The count's men know them too, and if they find you there it is the toll and half again.
We go down together and pay together and drink on it after. The bishop's people say we drink too early in the day. The bishop's people lost the battle.
Go down in the Tiel men's company and pay what the count's men ask: thirty pennies
Take the back creeks on the night tide
Hear the Tiel men out, and cut their count of it on your stick

The count's men take thirty pennies from you and more from the wine ships, and wave the company through by noon. A Tiel man tells you what this does to the price of Rhine wine at Lunden. You cut the count's toll on your stick.

Reeds on both sides and a hand's depth under her. You come out into the open river at first light with the count's fires well astern. You saw his post from behind, and you cut what you saw on your stick.
A boat is lying across the creek mouth with a lantern under a cloak. They are polite about it. The toll, and half again for the trouble of sitting up. You cut it on your stick with the rest.
They give it to you keel by keel: what was taken this year, from whom, and what was only called a gift. It takes a long stick. They say that if the emperor will not hear it, some other king might.

A river quay at dusk with broad Frisian trading ships loading casks side by side; a stout merchant pointing downriver, a skipper drawing creeks in the mud with a stick; far off across flat marsh, a small fort with a fire on its bank.
After the Holy River

This year the king went with his ships to the Holy River, and Ulf and Eglaf came against him out of Sweden by land and by sea. Very many were lost on the king's side, Danes and English both. The fleet is buying bread, and the wounded lie in the boat sheds.
Bread, salt meat, ale, cheese, whatever you have. The king pays a third over the market and pays in his own pennies. Do not ask me how many mouths. Fewer than a month ago.
Who won? The Svear kept the field. The king kept Denmark. You may call that as you like, but I would not call it anything in his hearing.
Godric, of Lunden, a rower in the king's pay. I keep the leg if I keep it dry, the leech says. Four of us from the Thames lie in this shed, and no ship goes home till spring.
They say the river came down on us all at once, timber and all. I did not see it. I saw the man next to me, and then I saw the sky.
Sell the fleet your bread, meat and drink at the king's price
Take Godric and three more home to the Thames, for nothing
Keep clear of a beaten fleet, and listen
The steersman takes all of it and pays ninety pennies over what the market would have given, new coin, counted not weighed. Every keel on this shore will be bringing bread here for a month.

They are carried down on a door, one by one. Godric says the shipmen of Lunden keep a long memory and a short list, and that you are on the list now. Your crew gives up the dry end of the boat without being asked.
You lie off and let others sell. By evening you know who is dead, who is said to be dead, and that the king is going to keep Christmas among the Danes. That is worth carrying home.

A Danish beach under low cloud: battered longships hauled up, one with a split strake; a steersman bargaining over sacks of bread; in the mouth of a boat shed a wounded man on straw, his thigh bound, looking out at a merchant's small ship.
What was taken, and by whom

The king means to be at Rome when the emperor is crowned, and he will not go with an empty mouth. A priest of his household sits in the church porch with wax tablets and asks every shipman what was taken from him on the roads, and by whom.
The king will speak with the emperor and with every lord who holds a road. He wants to know what his people pay, where, and to whom. Slowly, please. I write badly on wax.
Everyone tells me about the barriers in the mountains. I have the mountains forty times over. Was nobody ever robbed on level ground?
You have read a toll writing, I am told. Then say which of these tolls had a king behind it and which only a rope. No emperor will undo his own gifts.
A word, shipman. At Lunden we of Cologne pay our toll, and pepper at Christmas, and no gate is shut on us. If your king shows our emperor a list with Cologne on it, somebody will shut one.
I saw you on the bank with your stick. Two hundred pennies, and the stick goes on the fire. The mountains are grievance enough for one king.
Lay your tally sticks on his table and say all of it, before witnesses
Tell him what the pilgrims say of the barriers in the mountains
Take the Cologne man's two hundred pennies and leave the Rhine off the tablets

He calls two men out of the church to stand by, and you read your notches to him: the place, the toll, the taker. He fills three tablets and asks for your name and your port. The Cologne man leaves before you have finished.

You tell him what the pilgrims told you: the barriers, the snow, the men at each one. He writes a single stroke beside something he has already written, thanks you, and looks past you at the next man.

The stick burns well; it was good dry ash. You give the priest the mountains, like everybody else. The Cologne man pays in his own town's pennies and says there is a place for a sensible man at their board.

A church porch in low winter sun: a tonsured priest on a stool with a stack of wax tablets on his knee, a line of shipmen waiting; at the edge of the porch a well-dressed Rhineland merchant in a fur-edged cloak leans in to speak quietly to one of them.
Palms on their staffs
A Frisian keel out of the Rhine mouth, deep with people. They have dry palm leaves tied to their staffs, and one of them is shouting across the water about the king.
On Easter day, in Saint Peter's own church! The emperor was crowned, and our king walked out beside him, the king of the Burgundians on his other hand. I was behind a pillar, but I saw it.
And he asked for us. For us! That we go and come in peace, no barriers, no toll-takers, merchants and praying men alike. The emperor said yes. An abbot is riding home with it written.
I know that boat! Cologne, the toll bank, forty-five pennies! I prayed for you at the tomb by name, shipman, and I had it right. Come alongside. I have something of yours.
They have told it to me nine times since Tiel. I could say it in my sleep, and I think I have. Take some of them, for the love of God.
Take three of them aboard for the Thames: they have walked far enough
Lie alongside: the Dane from the toll bank at Cologne knows your boat
Wave, and hold your course

You have the whole of it before you raise the land, and you have it a month before any town does. Every weaver's son in England will want to see Rome next spring, and he will carry cloth to pay his way.

Toke hands a small bag across the gap between the boats: a pound of pepper, bought at Pavia with the price of the cloth you saved him. He says the road is open now, and that half of Jutland will be on it by spring with cloth to sell.
The shouting goes on a long time astern. Something about the king and the emperor. You will hear it soon enough, in harbour, with everyone else.

Open sea on a clear breezy day: a broad Frisian ship crowded to the rail with weathered pilgrims, palm fronds lashed to their staffs, one old man standing on a thwart with both arms raised, shouting across the water to the viewer's boat.
The king's letter

This year Abbot Lyfing came home from Rome with the king's letter, and it was read to the English in their own tongue. The king has spoken with the emperor and with King Rudolf, who holds the barriers in the mountains. His people, merchants as well as those who go to pray, shall go to Rome and come home in peace, free of the barriers and the toll-takers.
The king says: I spoke with the emperor and the lord pope and the princes there of the needs of all my people, English and Danes. And they granted it, and set their word to it.
He says also that his reeves shall do no man wrong for his sake, rich or poor. And that he will have plough-alms, tithes and Rome-penny paid before he lands. Kings come home from Rome like that.
You gave the king's priest your word when he asked. It was the word everybody gave. That is how a king knows a thing is true.
Your house is known here for more than its prices. I was told to remember that when the letter came.
The king bids us do right by those who use the sea. A reeve can do right in several ways. Tell me which you want, and ask once.
Ask for the king's writ of protection for your house and keel
Take the writ, and a reeve's man to keep your goods: you paid for others on the road
Ask for ground at the hythe, held under the king's peace
Ask for nothing written: take the road's first fruits, and a man at the hythe

A strip of parchment with a seal hanging from it: the king greets his reeves in friendship and tells them your house and keel are in his peace on both shores. Six hundred pennies come with it, for losses on the roads. The peace is as long as the king.

The writ, sealed, and nine hundred pennies for what you laid out for other people's wounds and tolls. The reeve gives you one of his own men to keep your goods at the hythe between sailings. He says the king likes a debt paid where men can see it.

The reeve walks you along the hythe and stops at a strip between two wine cellars. Twelve feet of waterfront, four witnesses, and six hundred and fifty pennies to build with. Ground does not die with a king.

The first merchants home by the open road sell at the hythe that week, and the reeve sees you served first: six pounds of pepper, a bolt of silk, and silver for the rest. One of his men will keep your goods here. Nothing is written, so nothing can be unwritten.

A crowd before a church door in summer light: an abbot in a travel-stained cloak reading aloud from a long parchment with a hanging seal, a reeve beside him, townspeople, shipmen and a few pilgrims with staffs listening, masts showing over the roofs behind.
The river in the letter

This year Abbot Lyfing came home from Rome with the king's letter, and it was read to the English in their own tongue. It speaks of the barriers in the mountains, as everyone knew it would. Then it speaks of the river road: of the bank at Cologne and the water below Tiel. The abbot looks up from the leaf to see who is listening.
The king says: and I spoke with the emperor of the river also, where my people are tolled three times between the sea and Cologne. And the emperor granted that this too should be amended.
He had your sticks read to him twice on the road, shipman. At Rome he laid them on the table in front of the emperor. An emperor does not often see a grievance he can count the notches on.
The archbishop of Cologne was standing behind the emperor's chair. He said the toll was old. The king said so were the pilgrims.
Of the count at the river mouth the emperor said only that he had sent an army once. But he gave his word for the king's men on that water, and the count will have heard it by now.
Your name is in this, and names travel. The toll men of that river will know the boat that cost them their thirds. Take your reward with that in mind.
Take the emperor's grant: your keel free of toll at Cologne
Take the grant and the king's word that you are worthy of a thegn's right
Take the king's writ of protection, good on the count's water
Ask for nothing with a seal on it: take silver, and ground at the hythe

A leaf in a Rhineland hand, with the emperor's sign at the foot: the bearer and his keel pay no toll at the bank of Cologne. Nine hundred pennies come with it from the king. The toll man there will read it slowly, and then he will read it again.

The emperor's leaf for Cologne, and eighteen hundred pennies. Then the abbot says the old rule aloud before the reeve: a merchant who has fared three times over the wide sea at his own cost is worthy of a thegn's right. The reeve says it has been a good deal more than three.

The king's writ, sealed: your house and keel are in his peace, and the emperor's word stands behind it on the water below Tiel. Eight hundred pennies with it. The count's men will wave you through, and will count your casks as you go by.

Eleven hundred pennies, and a strip of the hythe between two wine cellars, taken before four witnesses. No leaf, no seal. The river road is freer for everyone, and your part in it is a thing people say, not a thing they can find.

A crowd before a church door in summer light: an abbot lowering a long sealed parchment to look straight at the viewer, three notched tally sticks tucked under his arm; a reeve at his shoulder, a Rhineland merchant at the edge of the crowd turning away.
A place at the Cologne board

The king's letter has been read. It speaks of the mountains and of King Rudolf's barriers, and it does not speak of the Rhine. The men of Cologne trade as before, and at Christmas they bring the reeve his pepper, his gloves and his vinegar. They have kept a place for you at their board.
Sit. We said there would be a place, and we of Cologne keep our word, having so few other faults.
Your king got his mountains and our emperor kept his river. Every gate is open that was open before. That is the best kind of peace: the kind in which nothing happens.
I went free through the mountains, as the letter says. I paid twice on the Rhine coming home. Nobody had told the Rhine. Is that wine from there?
Do not mind her. Now: we owe you more than two hundred pennies, and we would sooner pay it in something that lasts. Choose.
Sit down among the emperor's men, and trade as one of them
Ask for a man of theirs at Cologne to keep your goods
Take the rest of what they owe you in pepper, and one of their pilots for the river

They move along the bench. Six hundred pennies, and from now on you buy and sell at the hythe under the emperor's men's law, and bring your share of the pepper at Christmas. The widow finishes her cup and goes out without looking at you.

Seven hundred pennies, and a cousin of his below the wall at Cologne who will keep your goods dry and your name out of the toll man's mouth. The widow finishes her cup and goes out without looking at you.

Five hundred pennies, ten pounds of pepper, and an old pilot of theirs who shows you every bar from Tiel to the wall. No seat. They seem relieved. The widow finishes her cup and goes out without looking at you.

A lamp-lit wine cellar by the hythe on a winter evening: Rhineland merchants on benches at a long board with cups, pepper sacks and a pile of grey gloves; an empty place on the bench; near the door an English widow with a pilgrim's staff watching them over her cup.
One man's peace

This year King Cnut died at Shaftesbury, on the morrow of Martinmas, and they carried him to Winchester. The shipmen of Lunden and the thegns north of the Thames have chosen Harold. The queen sits at Winchester with the housecarls. Harthacnut is in Denmark and does not come.
I am still the reeve. Ask me whose reeve at Easter, when I know. Until then I take the toll in the name of whoever turns out to have been king.
Your writ greets the reeves of a king who is under the floor of the Old Minster. It is a good writ. It wants a living man's word over it, and living men charge.
Your business with the emperor's people is no affair of ours. They say the old king's daughter is to marry the emperor's son. So Cologne at least will stay friendly, whoever sits here.
The leg held. I row for the town now, and it was the town's shipmen who chose this king. I told them about a boat that carried four of us home from the Holy River for nothing.
One peace from the Thames to the Sound, they used to say. It turns out it was one man. He had two sons living, and they will have half of it each, if they are lucky.
Buy the new lord's word over the old king's writing: a hundred and twenty pennies
Let the shipmen of Lunden speak for you: they remember who carried their wounded home
You hold of the emperor, not of a dead king: buy cloth while the English quarrel
Let the old writing lie in the chest: it was one man's peace

The reeve writes a line under the old king's greeting and presses a new seal beside the old one. A hundred and twenty pennies. He says the next king will want as much again, and that it is still cheaper than a toll.
Godric and eleven others come up from the ships and stand in the reeve's door. They do not say much. The reeve writes a line under the old king's greeting, seals it, and waves away your purse.

Nobody in Lunden is sure this month whose toll it is, so the weavers sell low and quickly, and Cologne has heard nothing yet. You fill the hold. An emperor's leaf does not care who is king of the English.

You put the old writing at the bottom of the chest. A priest on the hythe, who has seen four kings buried, writes you out a poem about men who lost everything and outlived it. Each verse ends the same way: that passed, and so may this.

A reeve's doorway on a raw November day, bare trees, a church bell tower behind: the reeve holding an old sealed writ up to the light, a group of oarsmen standing close by with their arms folded, one leaning on a stick; black cloth hung from the church door.
The tribute is weighed out in England: seventy-two thousand pounds, and ten thousand five hundred more from Lunden. The fleet goes home to Denmark, all but forty ships.
The king is sending English moneyers over the sea with their irons. Pennies with his face are to be struck among the Danes, to pass by count on both shores.
The king's fleet met the Svear and the Northmen at the Holy River. Very many were lost on his side, Danes and English. He keeps Christmas in Denmark.
The king's letter is read in England: the emperor and the king of the Burgundians have freed his people, merchants and pilgrims, of barriers and tolls on the road to Rome.
The English king's letter names the river road too. The emperor has given his word against the third toll on the Rhine, for the king's men, and the toll men are not pleased.
